newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: U.S. group focuses on regional Australian telecoms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. group focuses on regional Australian telecoms.

text.p: While Australia's major telecoms companies slug out for market share and profits in the country's big cities, one telephone group sees money to be made by focusing on provincial Australia towns.

U.S. owned Northgate Australia operates telephony and pay television services in the former gold mining town of Ballarat in the western part of the southern state of Victoria, but Northgate plans to expand to regional centres around Australia.

Northgate executive director Fred Buddemeyer said the group is interested in Newcastle and Wollongong in New South Wales, regional Queensland and Australia's biggest state, Western Australia, and its capital Perth.
"We think these are all markets that have big demand. There is less infrastructure, but there is more demand as people make more long distance phone calls," Buddemeyer told Reuters.

Buddemeyer said the take-up on pay-TV is about 20 percent, which is double the group's projection, but with its telephony services, customers are on a trial basis until Tuesday, when the Australian telecommunications market becomes fully deregulated.
"We project telephony take-up at about 10 percent, but looked at what happened with cable, so I think we are going to be in for a pleasant surprise," Buddemeyer said.

Ballarat is Northgate's first regional centre and the group plans to build out around the rest of western Victoria, to Geelong, Bendigo and Albury-Wodonga and Wagga Wagga in New South Wales, the American born executive said.

Telecoms analysts expect Australia's A$25 billion telecommunications market to be carved up by niche players on a geographical basis and also by segmentation through specialised services including the Internet or servicing ethnic markets.

Eventually Northgate plans to pass one million homes around Australia through its cable network carrying both telephony and pay TV services, within the next three to five years at a cost of about A$500 million, Buddemeyer said.
He said the A$500 million is going to be funded by its U.S. parent Northgate Communications, private shareholders, some strategic partners and through a public float.

"We would like to do a float within about 18 months," said Buddemeyer, adding "We would put the float within the hundreds of millions of dollars." He said the parent company may sell below a controlling interest through the proposed float.
"You will probably see a partner come in before the float ... but it depends on market conditions," he said.
Northgate Communications is privately held and has no plans for an IPO, Buddemeyer said.
A float of Northgate Australia will be one of many telecoms related share offerings over the next two years.
The Australian government plans to raise a minimum of A$8 billion later this year from the sale of a third of Telstra Corp Ltd through a public share issue.
Fellow carrier Optus Communications Pty Ltd is expected to raise around A$1.5 billion when it floats.

Other potential telecom share issues include U.S. controlled telecoms service group Worldxchange Pty Ltd and AAPT Telecommunications Pty Ltd, while the local arm of Vodafone Plc has an option to float by the year 2002.
"Eventually we could be looking at a very significant sector of the Australian (share) market," said one telecommunications analyst, who asked not to be named.
